en: The Accomplishment of Reality Following Manifest Phenomena, by the Yoginī Cintā. Homage to the glorious Vajrasattva!
Victorious is the unique King of Bliss, devoid of cause, ever-arisen for the worlds.
And at the time of whose proclamation even the Omniscient One became impoverished of words. || 1 ||

This specific instruction, arising from my long-standing and exceptional devotion to the feet of the most excellent Guru, has been written here by me for my own memory; what hostility toward wise people could there be in this? (2)

In this non-dual state, which is pure by nature, the Blessed One, having manifested for himself the form of a man and woman through his very self in its innate condition, and having projected his own form within his own forms for the sake of realizing that meaning, demonstrates here the reality that conforms to manifest existence: Through gazing upon the beautiful women created in his innate state, the Blessed One’s mind becomes desirous of the bliss of sexual union; then, from those women who possess exceedingly passionate and playful glances, and then from their very soft, tender, and heart-captivating sweet words...

Then, his heart opened by the intense fragrance of thick, fragrant ointments following after her; then, having had his heart captured, as if attaining the great bliss of being sprinkled from a hundred jars of nectar, he experienced the various modes of the pleasure of impetuous embraces; then, considering himself as one who has achieved his life’s purpose, he tasted, as it were, the incomparable flavors of the various types of endearing kisses; and thereafter, the specific varieties of biting and scratching with the teeth. Dispelling the singular birth of the bliss of celestial passion (*surata*) through the stimulation and awakening of the application of extremely soft fingernails, and further through the diversions of the manifold, thick, and warbling cooing of the cuckoo—by means of these natures, he himself carries out his own drama, which is like a fivefold dream. By this, the engagement in the practice of the movement for achieving the specific attainment of that mind is accomplished.
Then, with beloved and affectionate glances, followed by words dripping with honey, then with showers of love, and finally with the arrival of the sovereign flavors;
I do not know what remains of that sequence, nor who she was, nor who he was; O friend, some other bliss has arisen that cannot be reached by words. || 3 ||

This engagement in the practice of *sāgraha* (firm resolve) binds the mental continuities of both of you by means of this [practice], which obstructs the expansion of the arising of passion; thus, both mental continuities become focused on nothing else. Consequently, they become uninterrupted and indifferent to the merging of waters—tremulous with affection and eager for the festival currently unfolding in the singular flow of happiness.

Then, immediately thereafter, as if by force, the internal movement of their minds proceeded from the present enthusiasm through various modes of unpremeditated skillful action and many moans, resulting in the intensification of the great aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of the erotic passion (*surata*), which was entirely indifferent to all external concerns. Consequently, there arose a mass of the essence of worldly happiness, born from the intensification of the pleasure of enjoyment—a realm of self-realization beyond the senses—awakened by the practice of the blissful act of love through extreme familiarity.

That which is this bliss with signs (*sanimitta-sukha*) is itself the signless knowledge (*nimittaparihīṇa-jñāna*) of the worlds, the self-arisen form (*svayambhūrūpa*), great bliss (*mahāsukha*), devoid of conceptual construction (*kalpanāśūnya*), the mind in which the reality of latent impressions (*vāsanātattva*) arises.

From this [source], he who is the Lord of the World—the blissful self whose nature is pure *sattva*, radiant with a veil of all external conceptualizations cast aside, his mental continuum having become ungraspable, extremely flickering due to the latent impressions of the subtle continuity of the cycle of existence fashioned like an illusion, and whose state of being faltering in the midst of pleasure has been joined with time—descends together with drops of semen into the mother whose season has arrived; he enters the interior of the lotus at the base of the navel, which faces downward and has eight petals, where its tips are blossoming, and there he consumes the remaining blood that has flowed down.

He embraces her; immediately thereafter, a lotus bud arises there. Within that, the two constituent elements—red and white seed—blend together like milk and water according to their own nature and assume the form of a mass. This mass then undergoes a process of transformation through successive stages, beginning with the *kalala*, until it attains the accumulation and growth of all the primary elements (*bhūta*).

And wherever there is a conjunction (*samavāya*) of the five elements, earth and so forth, there that sensation (*vedanā*) manifests its distinct state; thus, like the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), the body came to consist of the nature of sensation. This [body] follows upon sensation and is determined by its specific conditions... [p. ...]

[172] Though it is truly all-pervasive and omnipresent, being conjoined with the extremely fickle great elements and the mind, it remains localized; though it is accessible to the village of the five external sense-faculties, it is overwhelmed by the state of subject and object regarding imagined external forms and so forth. Through delusion, it becomes a most voracious driver of the wheel of saṃsāra, accompanied by envy, stinginess, fear, grief, jealousy, shamelessness, lack of compassion, craving, and the pursuit of the desirable and undesirable.
This very mind, due to the causal karma performed in previous births, undergoes inclusion within this present birth.
It surely consumes everything entirely; it renders all things together with their latent impressions (vāsanā). || 4 ||
Thus concludes the exposition on the structure of cyclic existence.

For those transmigrating beings who do not, with supreme devotion, bow down for the sake of the ultimate good to the pair of lotus-feet of the Great Compassionate One—the noble one whose nature is supremely affectionate and full of mercy, who serves as a boat and raft for crossing this ocean of saṃsāra that is most terrible and difficult to cross; an ocean where the waters are the ego-sense, deep and unfathomable, filled with a succession of waves that rise and subside, and which is expanded by the fierce and harsh whirlwinds of mutual attraction and repulsion—[to them I speak].

They offer praise but do not serve; they do not produce contentment, and for them, no crossing over the ocean of insurmountable calamities is envisioned. Therefore, for the sake of the ultimate good (*niḥśreyasa*), the pair of lotus-feet of the true guru must at all times and in every way be venerated as the means to liberation. For if there were not gurus—who are like saving ships—to protect us from this most terrible, endless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) which is an ocean of objects difficult to restrain.

Why is this? Because, due to the abundance of the web of their own conceptual constructions and being agitated by the terrors [of saṃsāra], these people will attain here that Buddhahood which is the sole abode of supreme bliss. || 5 ||
Attending upon the True Guru

And because of his satisfaction with this instruction, one who—failing to understand that [the world] is exceedingly fickle and being overwhelmed by the entire collection of the senses—is intensely preoccupied with increasing incomparable sensual pleasures, becomes like a painter who, upon seeing his own painted picture of a fierce and singular form, falls into extreme despondency out of fear and succumbs to cowardice; even so, in this case as well, having constructed a mass of unreal mental fabrications, one becomes helpless, overcome by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) produced by actions characterized as desirable or undesirable, and thus practices one's own [true] nature.

Bearing the wheel of beginningless saṃsāra like a revolving wheel, while the universe has become subordinate, this vital breath (*prāṇa*), whose nature is consciousness and which abides in the elements, remains here. And it is drawn away from the senses and established in its own constant activity of the path of incessant inhalation and exhalation.

By this means, one becomes turned away from the dense mass of fresh thirst arising from the experience of various thick, divine, and fragrant fruits—great and manifold, produced by the intense fragrance of the pleasure of hearing [the Dharma], which generates the joy of the ripened fruit found on the tree of worldly existence that has grown far aloft through being watered and nourished by the abundant, restless, and sweet waters of the thick bed of all sorts of false conceptual nets. He, moreover, follows after that which is innate (*sahaja*). Abiding therein, he abandons everything that has gone outward.

Even there, because an innate activity persists, the fickle mind remains fixed while experiencing that very distraction. Furthermore, by perceiving with particularity even there, there would be no further passion for the experience of an object already experienced; therefore, this brings about a slackening of engagement.

What need is there for much? When this [consciousness], abiding in its own nature, has emerged from the external, conceptualized forms, it remains undifferentiated and abides in its own essential state (*svabhāva*). Even then, with its exertion broken by the fading of passion through engagement with its own limited objects, it becomes intent on resting in its own very *ālaya*. And in that state, since it possesses all qualities, stability (*sthairya*) would also be its quality; thus, it comes to possess the quality of steadfastness.

Just as a mass of clouds, deep with dense thundering that pervades the entire courtyard of the sky, dissolves away so that its departure is not perceived anywhere; even so, this wind of the mental continuum, having come to rest and now dissolving, attains supreme cessation and does not go anywhere at all.
Abiding in its own place, this innate wind, freed from the web of conceptual construction, being of the nature of emptiness, generates an indescribable satisfaction within one's own mind.
Because of these aforementioned causes—the manifold methods of great compassion—he necessarily becomes one who always acts for the benefit of infinite sentient beings within this saṃsāra. (6)
Stabilizing the Mind

And so let it be heard: when there is instability, from the approach of the senses arises contact with sense-objects; from contact with sense-objects arises the perception of things; and from the perception of things arises the difficult-to-cross cycle of existence, seized by the many crocodiles of the desirable and undesirable. But because of stability, one remembers the intellect—resplendent, whose nature is consciousness, which is free from the proliferation of specific births, and which is the supreme state of one's own innate nature.

And when he is embraced by her, then, having become blended like sky with sky in the expanse of space, there arises the Leader’s mind—whose object is a particular mode of birth, which was previously characterized by joy and delight; which is non-conceptual, free from mental construction, equal to the void, empowered by the empowerment of all mudrās, unborn, beyond the senses, the domain of one's own realization, inexpressible, and entirely distinct—the very nature of wisdom and means, whose essence is bliss.
When the wind follows the intellect, it possesses the form of bliss and brings satisfaction produced by one's own mind.
Apart from those two, there is something else, the Immovable One, whose nature consists of wisdom and means. (7)
The abiding state of the mind, which is the manifestation of reality consisting of wisdom and skillful means.

Those [senses] as well, having previously abandoned their respective faculties and being disengaged from the mind, become causeless and follow the mind alone, just as calves whose mothers have been abandoned follow their mother. Likewise here too, the senses, following the mind, operate wherever the mind is; for without it, they have no application at all.

Now, this is the distinction in that regard: when the collection of sense-faculties has entered into a state of unsurpassed enjoyment—having abandoned the entire array of conceptual constructions and having attained the light of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) arisen from wisdom and means—this very world attains a state of oneness with the flavor of the form of great bliss.

And just as the world appears like a reflected image, as if mirrored by the lunar orb awakened by the cluster of the sun's rays, so too, when the collection of causes is devoid of grasping and becomes intermingled with the mind, the entire universe—both moving and unmoving—would, through the glory of non-arising (*anutpāda*), become the very form of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) endowed with the wealth of incomparable aesthetic flavor.

By this very [statement], the following is expressed: having attained sovereignty over the world together with those sense-faculties—which have become concealed, are like nectar, and act in accordance [with his will]—the Lord, the Master, proceeds entirely by his own autonomy.

There, the sense faculties—though empty of grasping like those of a newborn infant—display a cleverness fashioned by the charming young attendants following him and enjoy that [object]. Therein, the leader, who is free from all conceptualization, naturally pure, and the very form of gnosis, proceeds having entered into the assembly of the senses which follow the manifest state of excellence.

If the mind itself were not thus one whose entire collection of sense-faculties has been swallowed up, from where then could this emerging universe arise? For there exists nothing higher than the mind, nor anything else that stands in opposition to it.
With its group of senses withdrawn, with conceptual constructions destroyed, and with the seed of existence no longer incomplete—ah!
how cool and sweet is this [state], which, though equal to the sky, shines with bliss! (8)
The mind of great bliss, bound by wisdom and means, [abides] within the collection of the senses that have become settled.

Alternatively, what is the use of this elaborate exposition intended for the instruction of the ignorant? If the mind itself does not possess the nature of a real entity (*vastu*), then from where could external objects arise? If, on the other hand, the mind itself possesses the nature of a real entity, even so, that mind is internal; thus, in every respect, there is no arising of external objects at all. Therefore, it is the mind alone—devoid of conceptual construction, free from arising and destruction, non-dual, and here of pure nature—that manifests in its entirety as the form of gnosis (*jñāna*).

By this it is meant: from the bodhicitta that is pure by nature, those very movements of the limbs that emerge simultaneously are all varieties of *mudrā*; and those movements of speech are varieties of *mantra*. Furthermore, that which is the simultaneous unfolding and vibration—unceasing, non-abiding, unconditioned, immeasurable, and manifesting as various forms, flavors, dispositions, and gestures, such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), the heroic (*vīra*), the loathsome (*bībhatsa*), and the furious (*raudra*)—[is the nature of the deity].

Furthermore, whether it be the comic, the terrifying, the pathetic, the marvelous, the peaceful, and so forth, or whatever arises—such as attachment, aversion, delusion, pride, arrogance, envy, or jealousy—all of that reflects back as the entirety of the aspect of pure intrinsic-nature gnosis. Thus, the entire triple world is mind; this is it. And so it is said:
"In one place its nature is compassion; in another, it is like a great *rākṣasa*; in one place it maintains silence; and in another, it displays incomparable loquacity."
In one place restless with craving, in another like a wish-fulfilling gem; in one place asleep in slumber, and in another vigilantly awake.
In one place content with sweets, in another finding satisfaction even in stale and putrid food;
in one place attached to passion, in another the sole abode of dispassion;
in one place established in virtuous conduct, and in another—alas!—the abode of wickedness.
In some places there is the onset of stability, and in others, a movement as flickering as lightning.

In one place he is reddened by passion for play, and in another he is solely devoted to the sentiment of humor; in one place his nature is unrestrained, and in another his movement is likewise bound; in one place he sits in a state of dejection, and in another he is pure, with a body cleansed by holiness.
In one place he is skilled at exposition, and in another he is singularly hardened by dullness.
In one place satisfied with little, and in another averse to contentment;
in one place possessed by the impulse to dance, his mental activity having become exceedingly lax; in one place excelling in song, and in another intent on loud lamentation.
In one place he is the locus of happiness, and in another, utterly helpless against suffering alone. || 12 ||
In one place he is intent on the vice of gambling; in another, he has ceased from it; in one place he is soiled with dust; in another, he is beautiful with a pleasant bath;
in one place he is naked; and in another, he is clothed in variegated garments.
In one place he is a giver and an enjoyer; in another, his mental state is as wretched as that of a beggar.

In one place he is a speaker of falsehoods, and in another he is one whose word is solely truth; in one place he is an array of righteousness, and in another he possesses the power to produce a mass of sin;
in one place he is puffed up with pride, and in another he is exceedingly compliant and most virtuous.
In some places he is a magician, and in others he is a person of pure and exalted intellect.
In some places he is the seer and in others the object seen; in some places his greatness is not attained, and in some places he has not reached the state of destruction.
In some places he abides within the elements, and in some places he transcends the elements.
In some places it has various forms, and in others it is beyond the scope of words.

In one place he is a site of disease, and in another, an abode of great bliss; in one place he is skilled at begging for alms, and in another, possesses the majesty of a great king; in one place he experiences the joy of yoga, and in another, he appears distinct, like an ordinary living being.
[Missing] || 16 ||

Thus, for that skillful one whose mind is established in this way— in the image (*bimba*) that is spontaneous, of the nature of the coemergent (*sahaja*), free from conceptual construction (*kalpa*), and without support—
this majesty of attaining the state of the Sugata is as if held in the palm of his hand.
The supreme state of true bliss, overflowing with love for the great undertaking. || 17 ||
Thus, the mind has a single flavor with bliss such as non-arising and so forth.
For this very reason: "The supreme essence of all entities, equal to all phenomena."
He is the all-knowing, the all-perceiving, the all-encompassing, who upholds the intrinsic nature of all phenomena. || 18 ||
Abiding in non-abiding nirvāṇa, acting for the benefit of the world, and impartial;
established in the nature of both the one and the many, yet devoid of intrinsic nature, he is the immovable Great One. 19.
The Blessed One is to be realized within oneself; the Lord is beyond all analogies.
He is omnipresent, all-pervading, the creator and the destroyer, the Lord of the world.
He is the glorious Vajrasattva, the illuminator of manifest existence. (20)

Thus ends the *Tattvasiddhi*, which follows the manifest state, flowing with abundant streams of the rain of nectar—the wealth of great bliss—trickling from the lotus-face that has blossomed impetuously through the commitment (*samaya*), empowered by the vajra-samādhi of the three worlds, arising from the true discourse on the reality of phenomena as it surges forth from the right curiosity of the assembly of Śrī Yoginīs, born of the self-arisen wisdom at the Great Vajra Seat of Śrī Oḍiyāna.

Having heard that the mind might thus be so influenced—that it would become discolored by the introduction of a grand assembly for the recitation of what was authorized and approved [by the Buddha]—and having entered the path of vision of those people devoted [to the Dharma], she appeared in manifest form; yet, although she had previously been active, she was long ago permitted [by the Blessed One] as something unarisen.

For one who has no reckoning by the hosts of elements, but only by the intellect purified within itself, there shall be this path beyond laughter through [the realization of] existence, and for him there is true happiness. Thus, the *Tattvasiddhi*, a boat upon the great ocean of the discipline of yoginīs, which is secluded and devoted to true happiness, has been written by me, Śubhasiddhā; may there be success for the three worlds!
The *Tattvasiddhi* is completed.
Thus ends the great secret of the treatise on the principles of books and mantras.
